title: Birational Morphisms, Contractions, and Surface Singularities

items.title: Exceptional curves of the first kind and their contractions
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice where it is inherited from the degree and intersection suppliers below.
Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme.

**(a) Exceptional curves of the first kind.** A closed subscheme $E\subseteq X$ is an *exceptional curve of the first kind* if it is an effective Cartier divisor on $X$ ([[def-effective-cartier-divisor]]), there is a field $\kappa$ and an isomorphism $\mathbb P^1_\kappa\to E$ of schemes, and the normal sheaf $\mathcal N_{E/X}=\mathcal O_X(E)|_E$ (equivalently the conormal sheaf $\mathcal O_X(-E)|_E$, [[def-invertible-sheaf-of-cartier-divisor]]) pulls back under that isomorphism to $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1_\kappa}(-1)$.

**(b) Contractions.** Let $E\subseteq X$ be an exceptional curve of the first kind. A *contraction of $E$* is a proper morphism $b\colon X\to X'$ such that $X'$ is Noetherian, there is a closed point $x'\in X'$ with $\mathcal O_{X',x'}$ regular of dimension $2$, and $X$ together with $b$ is the blowup of $X'$ at $x'$ ([[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]]), with $E$ identified with its scheme-theoretic exceptional fibre $b^{-1}(x')$. Thus a contraction is exactly, up to unique isomorphism over $X$, the inverse of the blowing up of a regular point of a surface.

**(c) Contraction notation.** If $f\colon X\to Y$ is a morphism of schemes and $E\subseteq X$ is an integral curve, we say $E$ is *contracted by $f$* if $f(E)$ is a single point of $Y$.

**(d) Dictionary on a regular projective surface.** Let $k$ be a field, $X$ an integral regular projective surface over $k$, and $E$ an integral effective Cartier divisor. If $E$ is $k$-isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1_\kappa$ for a finite extension $\kappa/k$, then $E$ is exceptional of the first kind exactly when $E\cdot E=-[\kappa:k]$. In particular for $E\cong\mathbb P^1_k$ the criterion is $E\cdot E=-1$. Here $\kappa=H^0(E,\mathcal O_E)$ is the constant field, not the function field $\kappa(E)$. Indeed the normal line bundle is $\mathcal O(d)$ for a unique $d$ by [[cor-picard-projective-line-integers]] and [[lem-uniqueness-of-twists-on-the-projective-line]]. The projective-space cohomology calculation gives $\chi_k(\mathbb P^1_\kappa,\mathcal O(d))=[\kappa:k](d+1)$, so its degree over $k$ is $[\kappa:k]d$. The restriction-degree identity [[thm-intersection-with-curve-as-degree-of-restriction]] therefore gives $E\cdot E=[\kappa:k]d$, and normal twist $-1$ is equivalent to the asserted intersection value.
items.strategy: Definition assembly. Part (d) uses the projective-line Picard classification, the arbitrary-field twisting-sheaf cohomology calculation, restriction of scalars multiplying dimensions by [κ:k], and the restriction-degree identity. No function field is identified with the constant field.

items.title: Fibres of a proper birational morphism of regular surfaces
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $X$ and $Y$ be integral regular finite-type $k$-schemes of pure dimension two, let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a proper birational morphism and let $y\in Y$ be a closed point. Put $F=f^{-1}(y)$. Then:

1. $F$ is a proper $\kappa(y)$-scheme with $\dim F\le 1$.
2. If $\dim F=1$, then $F$ has finitely many irreducible components $C_1,\dots,C_r$; each, with its reduced induced structure, is an integral proper curve over $\kappa(y)$ ([[def-integral-scheme]], [[lem-proper-fibres-proper]]); and each $C_i$ contains a closed point $x_i$ with $x_i\notin C_j$ for every $j\neq i$.
3. For every generic point $\xi$ of a one-dimensional component of $F$ the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,\xi}$ is a discrete valuation ring, and $f^\sharp$ identifies the function field of $Y$ with the function field of $X$.
4. The set $N(f)$ of integral curves $C\subseteq X$ with $\dim f(C)=0$ is finite. More precisely, the non-étale locus $Z\subseteq X$ of $f$ ([[def-etale-locus-morphism]]) is closed and not all of $X$, every contracted curve is contained in $Z$, and $N(f)$ is at most the number of irreducible components of $Z$.
5. If $f$ is not an isomorphism, then $N(f)>0$. Equivalently, if every fibre of $f$ is finite, then $f$ is an isomorphism.
items.strategy: Uses the arbitrary-scheme finite birational normal-target argument locally on affine opens, together with proper quasi-finiteness and regularity of the target.

items.title: Effective Cartier divisors on a regular scheme have no embedded associated points
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a regular locally Noetherian scheme and let $Z\subseteq X$ be an
effective Cartier divisor. Then every local ring $\mathcal O_{Z,z}$ is Cohen--Macaulay, of dimension
$\dim\mathcal O_{X,z}-1$. In particular $Z$ has no embedded associated points: if $s\in\Gamma(Z,\mathcal O_Z)$
vanishes at the generic point of every irreducible component of $Z$, then $s=0$.
items.strategy: At $z\in Z$ choose a local equation $t$ of $Z$; it is a nonzerodivisor in the regular local ring $\mathcal O_{X,z}$, and $\mathcal O_{Z,z}=\mathcal O_{X,z}/(t)$ has dimension $\dim\mathcal O_{X,z}-1$. The quotient of a Cohen--Macaulay local ring by a nonzerodivisor is Cohen--Macaulay ([[cor-regular-quotient-cohen-macaulay-equivalence]]), and $\mathcal O_{X,z}$ is Cohen--Macaulay because it is regular ([[def-cohen-macaulay-local-module-and-ring]]). Cohen--Macaulay modules have no embedded associated primes ([[cor-cohen-macaulay-modules-have-no-embedded-associated-primes]]); hence the associated primes of $\mathcal O_Z$ are the generic points of the components, and a section vanishing there is zero ([[def-associated-prime-of-a-module]]).

items.title: A nonzero section vanishing at a point forces positive degree
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $C$ be an integral proper $k$-scheme of dimension one and
let $\mathcal L$ be an invertible $\mathcal O_C$-module with a nonzero global section $s\in\Gamma(C,\mathcal L)$.
If $s$ vanishes at some closed point of $C$, then $\deg_C(\mathcal L)>0$ for the degree of
[[def-degree-invertible-sheaf-proper-dimension-one]].
items.strategy: A nonzero global section of an invertible sheaf on an integral curve has a nonzero generic germ and defines an injection $\mathcal O_C\to\mathcal L$: in every local frame its coefficient is nonzero in the domain. Its coherent cokernel $Q$ has zero generic stalk, hence finite support. At a closed point where the section vanishes the coefficient is a nonunit, so $Q$ has a nonzero stalk. A coherent sheaf of finite support has a finite filtration with skyscraper factors $\kappa(p)$: its annihilator cuts out a zero-dimensional Noetherian closed subscheme, its finite module decomposes into the finitely many Artinian local factors, and each has a composition series. Euler-characteristic additivity and the actual closed-point supplier give $\deg_C\mathcal L=\chi(C,Q)=\sum_p\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_{C,p}}Q_p[\kappa(p):k]>0$. This proves the full proper integral-curve claim without applying smooth geometrically integral Riemann–Roch suppliers beyond their hypotheses.

items.title: Completion base change preserves completed local rings on the closed fibre
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring, $\widehat A$ its maximal-adic completion, and $X$ a scheme locally of finite type over $A$. Put $Y=X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\operatorname{Spec}\widehat A$. The closed fibres of $X$ and $Y$ are canonically isomorphic. If $y\in Y$ lies on this fibre and $x$ is its corresponding point, then the local homomorphism $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ induces an isomorphism of maximal-adic completions.
items.strategy: Work in $X=\operatorname{Spec}B$, so $Y=\operatorname{Spec}C$ with $C=B\otimes_A\widehat A$ by thm-affine-fibre-product-tensor-ring. The completion quotient supplier gives $C/\mathfrak m^nC\cong B/\mathfrak m^nB$ for every $n\ge1$, including the closed-fibre identification at $n=1$. Let $\mathfrak p\subset B$ and $\mathfrak q\subset C$ represent corresponding fibre points. They contain $\mathfrak mB$ and $\mathfrak mC$, respectively, and are the same prime modulo these ideals. Since $\mathfrak m^nB\subset\mathfrak p^n$ and $\mathfrak m^nC\subset\mathfrak q^n$, the preceding isomorphism identifies $B/\mathfrak p^n$ with $C/\mathfrak q^n$. Localize at the corresponding primes, giving $B_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak p^nB_{\mathfrak p}\cong C_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak q^nC_{\mathfrak q}$ compatibly in $n$. Passing to inverse limits proves the assertion. AC is inherited from the completion suppliers; no new choice is used.

items.title: Dualizing biduality for finite algebras over a regular base
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $R$ be a regular Noetherian ring of finite dimension $d$, and let $B\ne0$ be a module-finite $R$-algebra. For any integer $s$, $D_B=R\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,R[s])$ is a dualizing complex over $B$. For every $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{fin}}(B)$ the canonical evaluation $M\to R\operatorname{Hom}_B(R\operatorname{Hom}_B(M,D_B),D_B)$ is an isomorphism; both duals are bounded with finite cohomology. These constructions commute with localization on $R$; localization on $B$ preserves the dualizing conditions and coherent bidual evaluation.
items.strategy: Every finite $R$-module has a bounded finite-projective resolution, by the finite global-dimension bound and Noetherian finite syzygies; truncation triangles give the same for bounded finite complexes. The invertible rank-one module $R$ has injective dimension at most $d$ by the global/injective dimension supplier. Resolve $R[s]$ by bounded injectives and apply $\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,-)$, which consists of injective $B$-modules by finite-ring coinduction. Thus $D_B$ has finite injective dimension; finite-projective resolutions of $B$ give finite cohomology. For a bounded finite $B$-complex $M$, coinduction gives $R\operatorname{Hom}_B(M,D_B)=R\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R[s])$ after forgetting $B$. The latter is bounded finite, since $M$ is finite over $R$. Applying the adjunction again identifies its double dual with the termwise double dual of a finite-projective $R$-resolution of $M$, canonically isomorphic to $M$. Evaluation under adjunction is the same signed termwise evaluation (at $1\in B$), so it is the actual $B$-bidual map; forgetting scalars detects quasi-isomorphisms. At $M=B$ this proves the homothety isomorphism. Finite resolutions give compatibility with $R$-localization. Over the Noetherian ring $B$, localization preserves bounded injectives: Baer's ideal test reduces this to localization of Hom from finitely presented ideals. It preserves finite cohomology and homothety, and coherent bidual evaluation localizes by a degreewise finite free $B$-resolution. Thus the local dualizing conditions hold. AC is inherited from resolutions. This extends the quotient-only supplier's proof to finite algebras without treating that supplier as already having the broader statement. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: Finite birational algebras descend across a flat completion neighbourhood
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $B\to C$ be a faithfully flat map of Noetherian domains and let $0\ne I\subset B$ be a finitely generated ideal such that $B/I^n\to C/I^nC$ is an isomorphism for every $n\ge1$. Let $C\subset C'$ be a finite birational algebra inside $\operatorname{Frac}C$, with $C'/C$ annihilated by a power of $IC$. Then there is a finite birational algebra $B\subset B'\subset\operatorname{Frac}B$, isomorphic to $B$ away from $V(I)$, and an isomorphism $B'\otimes_B C\cong C'$ as $C$-algebras.
items.strategy: Put $Q=C'/C$ and choose $n$ with $I^nQ=0$. Via $B/I^n=C/I^nC$, $Q$ is a finite $B$-module and $Q\otimes_BC=Q$. Resolve $Q$ by degreewise finite free $B$-modules; Noetherianity supplies each finite syzygy. Flatness and degreewise finite Hom give $\operatorname{Ext}_B^1(Q,B)\otimes_BC\cong\operatorname{Ext}_C^1(Q,C)$. The left Ext group is annihilated by $I^n$: multiplication on a projective resolution lifting a scalar that kills $Q$ is chain homotopic to zero, by successive projective lifts, and induces zero on Hom cohomology. Every module killed by $I^n$ is unchanged by tensoring with $C$, so the displayed map is itself an isomorphism. The class of $0\to C\to C'\to Q\to0$ therefore lifts to an extension $0\to B\to E\to Q\to0$; Ext-one classification gives an endpoint-preserving isomorphism $E\otimes_BC\cong C'$. The extension makes $E$ finite. Choose $0\ne a\in I$. Since $Q_a=0$, $E_a=B_a$; the map $E\to E_a$ is injective, as after the faithful flat base change any $a$-power torsion would vanish in the domain $C'$. Thus identify $E$ with a $B$-submodule of $B_a\subset\operatorname{Frac}B$ containing $B$. Its base change embeds in $B_a\otimes_BC=C_a$ and identifies there with $C'$, by the endpoint-preserving isomorphism localized at $a$. For $u,v\in E$, the product $uv\in B_a$ maps into $C'=E\otimes C$. The class of $uv$ in $(B_a/E)\otimes C$ is zero; faithful flatness makes the original class zero. Hence $uv\in E$. Give $B'=E$ this induced ring structure: its unit is the image of $1\in B$, and base change has exactly the ring structure of $C'$. The quotient is $Q$, so $B'=B$ away from $V(I)$. DC is retained from Ext-one classification and AC from degreewise finite resolutions. No abstract formal-gluing theorem is imported. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: Finite twisted resolutions over a regular local base
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $R$ be a regular Noetherian local ring of finite dimension $d$, $P=\mathbb P^N_R$, and $F$ a coherent sheaf on $P$. There is a finite resolution of $F$ by finite direct sums of twists $\mathcal O_P(m)$, of length at most $d+N+1$. Every bounded coherent complex on $P$ is perfect and belongs to the triangulated subcategory generated by these twists.
items.strategy: Set $S=R[x_0,\ldots,x_N]$, graded in the variables. The published graded-section finiteness supplier applies to this arbitrary Noetherian base: a sufficiently high truncated section module $M$ is finite graded over $S$. The section-extension argument identifies $\widetilde M=F$ on each standard open by $u/x_i^n\mapsto u/x_i^n$; truncation does not affect this localization because one can multiply numerator and denominator by a sufficiently high power of $x_i$. Resolve $M$ successively by finite graded free modules, using Noetherian kernels. The regular polynomial-ring global-dimension bound gives $\operatorname{pd}_S M\le d+N+1$, so the terminal syzygy $K$ is a finite graded projective $S$-module. Its quotient $K/S_+K$ is finite projective over the local ring $R$, hence free: lift a residue-field basis to a finite free cover by Nakayama, split the cover, and apply Nakayama to its kernel, which has zero residue quotient. Choose homogeneous lifts of a finite homogeneous $R$-basis. They define a finite graded free cover $G\to K$: its cokernel vanishes by bounded-below graded Nakayama (a least nonzero degree cannot equal a sum of positive-degree multiples). An ungraded projective splitting can be made degree zero by taking homogeneous components; its graded kernel is finite and is zero modulo $S_+$, so the same argument makes it zero. Thus $K$ is graded free. Sheafify the finite graded free resolution: localization and taking degree zero are exact, as is the affine associated-sheaf equivalence, so it becomes the claimed twist resolution. Finite truncation triangles give the statement for bounded coherent complexes. This adapts the field-only twisted-resolution proof at exactly its changed step: the degree-zero quotient is free over the **local regular base**, rather than a vector space. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: Normal scheme modifications and normalized point blowups
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the blowup and scheme-construction suppliers.

**Normal schemes.** A locally Noetherian scheme is *normal* if every local
ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is an integrally closed domain
([[def-normal-noetherian-ring]]). This is a local condition on the local
rings and is checked on an affine open cover; it does not require the global
section ring to be a domain. The empty scheme is normal vacuously.

**Normalization of an integral scheme.** Let $S$ be an integral scheme with
function field $K=K(S)$ ([[def-integral-scheme]]), and let
$\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$ be a nonempty affine open subset. Write
$\overline A$ for the integral closure of $A$ in $K$, that is, the subring of
elements of $K$ that are integral over $A$. The *normalization* of $S$ is the
$S$-scheme

$$\nu\colon S^\nu\longrightarrow S$$

obtained by gluing the affine schemes $\operatorname{Spec}\overline A$ over
the nonempty affine open subsets $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq S$, inside
the common function field $K$. This is well defined: by
[[thm-integrality-commutes-with-localisation]] the formation of $\overline A$
commutes with localization, so for a principal open
$D(f)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}A$ the canonical map
$(\overline A)_f\to\overline{A_f}$ is an isomorphism onto the integral closure
of $A_f$ in $K$; the affine integral-closure algebras therefore identify on
overlaps inside $K$ and satisfy the cocycle identity, and
[[lem-relative-spec-glues-affine-algebras]] constructs the glued scheme and
its canonical morphism to $S$. The scheme $S^\nu$ is integral, $\nu$ is
affine, and $K(S^\nu)=K$; the normalization is characterized up to unique
isomorphism over $S$ by this construction. *Finiteness of the normalization*
— that $S^\nu\to S$ is a finite morphism — is an additional assertion about
$S$ and is never part of the definition; it is proved separately on this
page for the surfaces that occur below.

**Modifications.** Let $S$ and $X$ be integral schemes. A *modification* of
$S$ is a proper morphism $f\colon X\to S$ ([[def-proper-morphism]]) that
induces an isomorphism $K(S)\to K(X)$ of function fields, so that $f$ is
birational. A *regular resolution* of $S$ is a modification $f\colon X\to S$
whose source $X$ is regular (all local rings regular). The modulus here is a
property of the morphism $f$, not of the source alone: the same scheme $X$
may occur as source of modifications of several different integral schemes.

**Point blowups and their normalization.** Let $S$ be a locally Noetherian
integral scheme ([[def-locally-noetherian-and-noetherian-scheme]]) and let
$s\in S$ be a closed point whose ideal sheaf $\mathcal I_s\subseteq\mathcal O_S$
is coherent and nonzero. The *point blowup of $S$ at $s$* is the blowup
$\operatorname{Bl}_s(S)\to S$ of $S$ along $\mathcal I_s$
([[def-blowup-scheme-along-ideal]]). It is locally projective, hence proper, over $S$; a single global
projective-space embedding is asserted only when the additional
global-generation or projective-base hypotheses are available. The *normalized point blowup of $S$ at $s$* is the composite

$$\operatorname{Bl}_s(S)^\nu\longrightarrow\operatorname{Bl}_s(S)\longrightarrow S ,$$

that is, the point blowup followed by normalization of its source. It is a
morphism of integral schemes. It is proper when the normalization morphism
$\operatorname{Bl}_s(S)^\nu\to\operatorname{Bl}_s(S)$ is finite; no
properness assertion is made when that finiteness has not been established.
The finite-normalization results below verify this condition in the surface
classes used in the resolution arguments.

**Resolution by normalized point blowups.** A *resolution of $S$ by
normalized point blowups* is a morphism
$X=S_n\to S_{n-1}\to\cdots\to S_0=S^\nu\to S$ obtained as follows: start with the
normalization $S_0:=S^\nu$ of $S$; choose
closed points $s_i\in S_i$ for $i=0,\dots,n-1$, each with nonzero coherent
point ideal, and let $S_{i+1}$ be the normalized point blowup of $S_i$ at
$s_i$; require that each normalization in the sequence, including the
initial normalization $S^\nu\to S$, be finite, and that the terminal scheme
$S_n$ be regular. Each arrow $S_{i+1}\to S_i$ is then a modification, the
composite is proper, and the terminal scheme is a regular resolution of
$S$. If $S$ is already normal, the initial normalization
$S^\nu\to S$ is an isomorphism, so the definition then starts effectively at
$S$ itself; if $S$ is regular, the empty sequence $n=0$ with
$S_0=S^\nu=S$ exhibits the identity as a resolution by normalized point
blowups.
items.strategy: Integral closure commutes with localization, so the affine integral-closure algebras identify on principal overlaps inside the common function field and satisfy the cocycle identity. The relative-Spec gluing supplier constructs their scheme and canonical map. Normality is the local algebra condition. A locally Noetherian scheme has coherent point ideals; the nonzero ideal gives a projective ordinary blowup. The normalized blowup is proper only when its normalization is finite, a condition established for the surface classes used in the resolution route.

items.title: Finite schemes over projective schemes are projective over a Noetherian affine base
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $R$ be Noetherian, let $X$ be projective over $R$, and let $Y\to X$ be finite. Then $Y\to X$ admits a closed immersion into one relative projective space over $X$, and $Y$ is projective over $R$. Finite compositions of projective morphisms between such schemes are projective.

items.title: CM local codimension and Ext concentration over a regular local ring
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice, inherited from
the resolution and Ext suppliers below ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian
Cohen--Macaulay local ring of dimension $D$.

**(a) Codimension formula.** For every prime $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$,

$$D=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim R/\mathfrak p .$$

Consequently $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=D-\dim R/\mathfrak p$, and for
every ideal $I\subseteq R$ with $R/I\ne0$ one has
$\operatorname{ht}I=D-\dim R/I$.

**(b) Concentration over a regular base.** Now assume in addition that $R$ is
regular, let $I\subseteq R$ be an ideal with $B:=R/I\ne0$, and assume that $B$
is Cohen--Macaulay of dimension $e$. Put $c:=D-e$. Then

$$\operatorname{Ext}^q_R(B,R)=0\qquad(q\ne c),$$

and $E:=\operatorname{Ext}^c_R(B,R)$ is a nonzero finite $B$-module which is
Cohen--Macaulay of dimension $e$ (over $B$, equivalently over $R$) and has
full support: $\operatorname{Supp}_B(E)=\operatorname{Supp}_B(B)=V(I)\subseteq
\operatorname{Spec}B$. No hypothesis is made on the number of generators of
$I$ or on the characteristic.

**(c) Localization.** The assertions localize: for every prime
$\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$ the ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is
Cohen--Macaulay of dimension $D-\dim R/\mathfrak p$; and if $R$ is regular and
$\mathfrak p\supseteq I$, then $B_{\mathfrak p}$ is a nonzero finite
Cohen--Macaulay $R_{\mathfrak p}$-module of dimension
$e_{\mathfrak p}:=\dim_{R_{\mathfrak p}}(B_{\mathfrak p})$, and
$\operatorname{Ext}^q_{R_{\mathfrak p}}(B_{\mathfrak p},R_{\mathfrak p})=0$
for every $q\ne\dim R_{\mathfrak p}-e_{\mathfrak p}$.
items.strategy: The depth-localization inequality gives $D\le\operatorname{depth}R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim R/\mathfrak p\le\dim R_{\mathfrak p}+\dim R/\mathfrak p$. Concatenating chains below and above $\mathfrak p$ gives the reverse inequality, proving the dimension formula without a separate catenarity import. For regular $R$, Auslander–Buchsbaum gives $\operatorname{pd}_RB=D-e=c$, so Ext vanishes above $c$. The dimension formula gives height $I=c$. Inductively choose $f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I$ regular: after $j<c$ choices the quotient $Q=R/(f_1,\ldots,f_j)$ is CM of dimension $D-j$; every associated prime of $Q$ has quotient dimension $D-j$, hence height $j$ in $R$. None contains $I$, so prime avoidance gives the next regular element. To check its parameter hypothesis, a regular element avoids every minimal support prime: chains in its quotient acquire one extra strict inclusion by prepending a minimal support prime, giving quotient dimension at most $\dim Q-1$. Conversely a shortest parameter tuple on that quotient, lifted and prepended by the element, makes a finite-length quotient of $Q$, so $\dim Q$ is at most one plus the quotient dimension. Thus dimension drops exactly one and the element extends to a system of parameters. The regular-parameter-quotient CM supplier now applies and preserves CM. For a regular element $f$ annihilating $B$, its two-term resolution and coinduction give $\operatorname{Ext}_Q^q(B,Q)=\operatorname{Ext}_{Q/fQ}^{q-1}(B,Q/fQ)$. Repeat through the regular tuple to get zero Ext below $c$. Dualize a finite free $R$-resolution of $B$ of length $c$; concentration makes its dual an exact resolution ending in $E$, so $\operatorname{pd}_RE\le c$. It is nonzero by canonical ambient biduality, and support lies in $V(I)$, hence dimension at most $e$. Auslander–Buchsbaum and the depth bound give $e\le\operatorname{depth}_RE\le\dim E\le e$, so it is CM. At any localization of $B$, a zero canonical module would make its dualizing complex zero and contradict homothety for the nonzero local ring, so support is full. The same finite resolutions and coinduction localize, giving the local conclusions. This generalizes the published field-polynomial Ext-concentration supplier by proving the missing codimension formula from an actual general CM supplier.

items.title: Surface p basis subfield separation
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $k$ have characteristic $p>0$, $A=k[\![X_1,\ldots,X_n]\!][Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}A$. Choose a possibly infinite $p$-basis $(b_i)_{i\in I}$ of $k/k^p$, meaning its restricted monomials of finite support form a $k^p$-basis. For finite $J\subset I$ put $k_J=k^p(b_i:i\notin J)$, $A_J=k_J[\![X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]\!][Y_1^p,\ldots,Y_m^p]$ and $K_J=\operatorname{Frac}A_J$. Then $A$ is finite free over $A_J$, the family $(K_J)$ is downward directed with intersection $K^p$, and for every finite field extension $L/K$, $\bigcap_J L^pK_J=L^p$.
items.strategy: For a possibly infinite family, p-independence means independence of its restricted monomials of finite support. Zorn supplies a maximal such family: its monomial span is a field, since each finite subfamily generates a finite exponent-one extension; any element outside that field would have degree p over it and extend the independent family. Thus maximality gives a p-basis b_i of k over k^p. For finite J put k_J=k^p(b_i:i outside J). The p-monomials on J form a finite basis of k/k_J. Together with X- and Y-monomials of exponents

items.title: Surface derivations and regular hypersurfaces
items.statement: Assume AC. Derivations of Noetherian rings extend uniquely through localization and adic completion. If $T$ is regular Noetherian, $D:T\to T$ a derivation and $D(f)$ a unit, then $T[z]/(z^r-f)$ is regular for every $r\ge1$. More generally, if $h\in T$ and $D(h)$ is a unit of $T/(h)$, then $T/(h)$ is regular.
items.strategy: D(I^n)⊂I^(n-1) gives a compatible map on inverse limits, whose Leibniz identity follows modulo every I^n; the localization quotient formula gives the other extension. Extend D to T[z] with D(z)=0. At a local ring with maximal ideal n containing z^r-f, membership of z^r-f in n² would imply its derivative belongs to n, whereas that derivative is -D(f), a unit. Thus the equation is part of a regular system of parameters, and its quotient is regular. Polynomial regularity and localization regularity are needed here. Exact source/proof evidence is retained in the normal-completion-sources helper packet; AC and DC inherited from the used suppliers are explicit.

items.title: Surface finite completion factors
items.statement: Assume AC. For a finite map $R\to S$ of Noetherian rings and $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$, $\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_RS\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak p}\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q}}$. The finitely many factors use their maximal-adic completions. Thus formal fibres for finite extensions are factors of residue-field base changes of the original formal fibres.
items.strategy: Finite-module completion is tensoring by R_p^hat. For each n, S_p/p^nS_p is Artinian and is the product of its localizations at the finitely many q over p; take inverse limits. In each factor the radical of pS_q is qS_q, so the two adic topologies are equivalent. Quotients commute with completion by exactness. In particular formal fibres for a finite ring extension are factors of residue-field base changes of the old formal fibres. Tensor/completion compatibility itself follows by taking a finite presentation R^a→R^b→S→0: exact completion gives the same cokernel as tensoring that presentation by the completed ring. Artinian product decomposition is the Chinese remainder decomposition into the powers of its finitely many maximal ideals; their sufficiently high product is zero. Thus no unproved finite-completion tensor formula is being hidden. items.title: Surface geometric regularity field test and generic spread
items.statement: Assume AC. For a Noetherian $k$-algebra $T$, call $T$ geometrically regular if $T\otimes_kE$ is regular for every finitely generated field extension $E/k$. It suffices to test finite purely inseparable $E/k$. Geometric regularity is stable under finitely generated field extension. If $K/k$ is finitely generated, finite purely inseparable enlargements $K'/K$ and $k'/k$ make $K'/k'$ separably generated. A separably generated generic fraction-field extension of finite-type domains spreads to a nonempty standard smooth open after localizing the base and source.
items.strategy: Choose a transcendence basis y for K/k and the maximal separable intermediate field M of K/k(y). If K/M has positive inseparable degree, choose β∈K\M with α=β^p∈M. Write the separable minimal polynomial P of α over k(y). Adjoin to k pth roots of the finitely many coefficients of the numerator and denominator polynomials expressing coefficients of P, and replace each y by y^(1/p). All coefficients of P now have pth roots in k′(y^(1/p)); taking coefficient roots gives a separable polynomial Q whose pth power is P(T^p). Thus the unique pth root β of α lies in a separable extension of the new rational field: Q(β)=0 and Q′(β)≠0. In the compositum K′, the inseparable degree therefore decreases by at least p. Repeat finitely; degrees multiply and all extensions made are finite purely inseparable. In characteristic zero there is nothing to do. For separably generated K/k, choose its separating transcendence basis y and a primitive separable generator θ. Clearing finitely many denominators makes its monic minimal polynomial P have coefficients in R[y]_a for a domain base R with k=Frac(R). Invert P′(θ). The algebra (R[y]_a[θ])_(P′) is a standard smooth algebra over R, and lies inside K; its injection follows by monic polynomial division and minimality over k(y). Given any finite-type R-subalgebra S⊂K with fraction field K, choose a common open containing y,θ and their inverses: the elements y,θ are fractions of elements of S, so first localize S to contain them. Conversely each of its finitely many generators and inverted denominators is a fraction in the standard smooth algebra, so invert their finitely many denominators there. The resulting two localized algebras agree inside K and are a nonempty standard smooth open of S after possibly restricting R. Published standard-smooth flatness and geometric-fibre regularity, together with flat-local regular ascent, prove regularity over a regular base. For the field test, take arbitrary finitely generated E/k and finite inseparable E′/E, k′/k as above. By hypothesis T⊗k k′ is regular. The standard smooth fraction-field model of E′/k′ makes T⊗k E′ regular by smooth ascent and localization. The map T⊗k E→T⊗k E′ is faithfully flat; published flat-local regular descent makes T⊗k E regular. This proves the test and also stability under finitely generated residue-field extensions. Exact source/proof evidence is retained in the normal-completion-sources helper packet; AC and DC inherited from the used suppliers are explicit.

items.title: Flat base change for quasi-coherent surface cohomology by Čech
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. For a quasi-compact separated scheme $X$ over a ring $A$, a quasi-coherent sheaf $F$ and a flat $A$-algebra $C$, the canonical maps $H^q(X,F)\otimes_AC\to H^q(X_C,F_C)$ are isomorphisms for every $q$. No flatness of $F$ over $A$ is required.
items.strategy: Choose a finite affine cover of X. Separatedness makes its finite intersections affine, so its Čech complex computes quasi-coherent cohomology by the named comparison theorem. Base-changing each affine intersection replaces its section module by its tensor with C, by the affine quasi-coherent equivalence and the fibre-product tensor formula. The finite Čech complex of the base change is therefore the original complex tensored with C. Flat tensoring preserves cycles, boundaries and their quotient, yielding the stated canonical isomorphisms. All identifications are restrictions and tensor maps, hence natural and compatible with cohomology boundary maps. The same argument for localization identifies higher-direct-image stalks at a base point with the cohomology over its local spectrum.

items.title: Reduced Cartier multiples on a normal local surface
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. If $A$ is a normal two-dimensional Noetherian local domain and $0\ne a\in\mathfrak m$, there is $c\in\mathfrak m$ such that $A/cA$ is reduced and $a\mid c^n$ for some positive integer $n$.
items.strategy: Let p1,...,pr be the finite height-one primes containing a. Begin with nonzero f in their intersection and complete f to a parameter pair (f,g). Since m^u⊂(f,g), for h∈m^(u+1) write h=αf+βg with α,β∈m; then (f+h,g)=(f,g). Hence all these perturbations have the same quotient length ℓ. Each Q=A/(f+h) is one-dimensional CM, with g regular. Its prime filtration gives χ(g,Q)=length(Q/gQ)=ℓ: the two-term multiplication-by-g Euler characteristic is additive by its exact homology sequence; zero-dimensional factors have equal kernel/cokernel length and contribute zero, and each one-dimensional prime factor contributes length((A/P)/g)≥1 because g is a nonzero parameter on it. Every minimal prime occurs in the filtration, by localizing that filtration at the prime. Thus Q has at most ℓ minimal primes. Choose h in m^(u+1)∩p1∩...∩pr maximizing that number and replace f by f+h. Let q1,...,qs be its height-one primes and mj=v_qj(f). For each j choose aj∈qj with valuation one and outside all other q's. For an explicit construction, choose bj∈qj with valuation one, possible because qj localizes to its DVR maximal ideal; choose cj∈qj outside all other q's by finite prime avoidance. If cj has valuation one, use it. Otherwise choose dj in the product of the other q's and outside qj (choose one element of each other prime outside qj and multiply). Then aj=cj²+bj dj has valuation one at qj; at every other q the first summand is a unit and the second vanishes. This gives the required aj. Set h′=∏_(mj=1)aj^2 ∏_(mj>1)aj. Multiply it by an element of m^(u+1) outside all qj, obtained by finite prime avoidance. Then f+h′ has valuation one at every qj. Maximality of s excludes any new height-one prime. The quotient A/(f+h′) is CM, so its associated primes are these minimal primes; its associated localizations are fields because all valuations are one. Associated-prime detection makes it reduced. Put c=f+h′. Its divisor contains all primes of a with multiplicity one, so for n≥max v_pi(a), c^n/a belongs to every height-one localization and therefore to A by the normal intersection supplier.

items.title: A rank-one surface module is principalized by an ideal blowup
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. For a finite torsion-free rank-one module $M$ over a Noetherian domain $A$, there is a nonzero ideal $J$ and a blowup $b:Y=\operatorname{Bl}_J\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ such that $b^*M$ modulo torsion is invertible; the same holds on every integral model dominating $Y$.
items.strategy: Choose an identification M⊗Frac(A)=Frac(A). Torsion-freeness embeds M in that field. Clear denominators in a finite generating family to identify M, up to multiplication by one nonzero scalar, with a nonzero ideal J⊂A. The ordinary blowup universal construction makes JO_Y invertible. The map b*M→JO_Y is generically an isomorphism, so its kernel is torsion. On every integral affine chart any element of its kernel is killed by a nonzero scalar (clear its zero generic germ); conversely any torsion element maps to zero in the invertible torsion-free module. Thus the kernel is exactly torsion and the quotient is invertible. Pulling further to an integral dominating model gives the same argument with the invertible pullback ideal. This uses a fractional ideal and the blowup universal property, not a general Fitting or flattening theorem.

items.title: Reflexive surface modules and codimension-one lattice extension
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. On a regular Noetherian surface a coherent reflexive module is locally free. For a finite module $M$ over a normal Noetherian domain, a generic vector belonging to $M^{**}$ at every height-one localization belongs to $M^{**}$. For a coherent generic-rank-$r$ module on a regular surface, $(\wedge^rM)^{**}$ is the determinant line of $M^{**}$.
items.strategy: From a finite presentation of M, dualization embeds M* as the kernel of a map between finite free modules. Over a regular local ring of dimension two the image of that map is torsion-free, so has depth at least one; the long exact Ext/depth lemma gives depth(M*)≥2. Apply the same argument again to M**, and Auslander–Buchsbaum makes this finite depth-two module free. In dimensions zero or one the regular local rings are fields or DVRs and finite torsion-free modules are free. A reflexive M equals M**, giving local freeness. For the second assertion write M**=Hom(M*,A). A generic vector v defines a generic functional on M*. If it belongs to all height-one M**, then for every φ∈M*, φ(v) belongs to every height-one A localization and therefore to A by normal intersection. Hence v defines a genuine element of Hom(M*,A)=M**. The same reasoning shows generic maps into a reflexive target extend when regular in codimension one. Modulo torsion, M→M** is an isomorphism at each DVR localization; its quotient is supported at closed points of a surface. Taking top wedges thus agrees in codimension one with det(M**), and the just-proved reflexive extension criterion identifies their double duals with that invertible determinant. The depth lemma here follows directly by applying Ext from the residue field to 0→kernel→free→image→0: Ext0(image)=0, Ext0,1(free)=0, so Ext0,1(kernel)=0.

items.title: A fixed-coordinate point-blowup chain defines a formal arc
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $(B,\mathfrak m,\kappa)$ be an equicharacteristic Noetherian local domain and $(B_n,\mathfrak m_n)$ the local rings at a successive infinite chain of point blowups, all with residue field $\kappa$. Suppose one $t\in\mathfrak m$ generates the pullback of every centre ideal on the next local ring. Then there is a nonsingular formal arc $B\to V$, extended from a surjection $\widehat B\to V$, whose point-blowup centres are the given ones. Here $V$ is a complete DVR with residue field $\kappa$ and uniformizer the image of $t$; no chosen coefficient-field identification is needed.
items.strategy: Embed every local blowup ring B_n in the common fraction field; the transition maps are injective and local. Their union U is a local domain with maximal ideal n=∪m_n and residue field κ. Because m_n B_(n+1)=tB_(n+1), every element of n is divisible by t in U; conversely tU⊂n. Thus n=tU. Cancellation in the domain and noninvertibility of t show t^j∉t^(j+1)U. Each successive quotient t^jU/t^(j+1)U is therefore isomorphic to U/tU=κ. Consequently U/t^N U is a local Artinian ring of length N. Put V=lim_N U/t^N U. Its kernel of reduction to κ is tV: divide each compatible element of that kernel by t modulo t^(N−1), where division is unique because U is a domain, and take the compatible limit. The t-adic intersection in V is zero by construction, and all powers of t survive. Every nonzero element has a finite first nonzero order N and is t^N times a unit; units are precisely elements with nonzero residue, their inverses given by successive lifting in the complete ring. Orders add under multiplication, so V is a domain. Every nonzero ideal is generated by an element of its least occurring order, and hence is (t^N); thus V is Noetherian, regular of dimension one and a complete DVR. The inclusions B_n→U→V are local and agree on residue fields. Their images of centre ideals are exactly (t), so the induced arc lifts to every point blowup with exactly the prescribed centre; this also follows from the blowup universal property and the local ring maps. The map B→V is continuous for the maximal/t-adic topologies and extends to Bhat by completeness. It is surjective: for v∈V successively choose c_i∈B lifting the residue of (v−Σ_(j<i)c_j t^j)/t^i. Then the series Σ c_i t^i converges in Bhat and maps to v. Its uniformizer t is the image of an element of m, making the arc nonsingular. This direct-union proof supplies the actual local lifts and surjection and avoids an unproved passage from quotient length counts to a completion quotient.

items.title: Universal property and uniqueness of a contraction
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the blowup suppliers. Let $X$ be a Noetherian scheme,
$E\subseteq X$ an exceptional curve of the first kind and $b\colon X\to X'$ a contraction of $E$
([[def-exceptional-curve-and-contraction]]). Write $x'=b(E)\in X'$. Then:

1. $b$ is proper, surjective and closed; $b\colon X\to X'$ is a topological quotient map identifying $X'$ with the quotient of $X$ obtained by collapsing $E$ to $x'$; the canonical map $\mathcal O_{X'}\to b_*\mathcal O_X$ is an isomorphism and $R^1b_*\mathcal O_X=0$.
2. (Universal property) For every morphism $\varphi\colon X\to Y$ of schemes with $\varphi(E)$ a single point there is a unique morphism $\varphi'\colon X'\to Y$ with $\varphi=\varphi'\circ b$.
3. (Uniqueness) If $b_i\colon X\to X_i'$, $i=1,2$, are contractions of $E$, there is a unique isomorphism $X_1'\to X_2'$ compatible with $b_1$ and $b_2$.

Consequently a contraction of $E$, when it exists, is unique and is characterized by the universal property.
items.strategy: By definition $b$ is the blowup of the regular point $x'$; such a blowup is proper, an isomorphism off the center, and its exceptional curve is $E$ ([[thm-blowup-projective]], [[lem-blowup-isomorphism-off-center]]). A proper surjective morphism whose target is obtained by collapsing one fibre is submersive, so $X'$ carries the quotient topology; [[lem-blowup-point-pushforward-vanishing]] gives $\mathcal O_{X'}\cong b_*\mathcal O_X$ and $R^1b_*\mathcal O_X=0$ for point blowups, hence for the contraction. For (2) define $\varphi'$ on the quotient topologically and use the adjunction between $b^{-1}$ and $b_*$: the map $\varphi^\sharp\colon \varphi^{-1}\mathcal O_Y\to\mathcal O_X$ is adjoint to a map $(\varphi')^{-1}\mathcal O_Y\to b_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{X'}$; locality at $b(E)$ is checked by noting that a function vanishing at $\varphi(E)$ pulls back to a function vanishing on $E$, hence vanishes at $x'$. Part (3) is immediate from (2) applied in both directions, and lands in the definition of contraction as a blowup up to unique isomorphism ([[cor-blowup-unique-up-to-unique-isomorphism]]).

items.title: Blowing up a regular point is a contraction
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $S$ be an integral regular finite-type $k$-scheme of pure dimension two, let $p\in S$ be a closed point, let $\pi\colon S'=\operatorname{Bl}_pS\to S$ be the blowup of $S$ at $p$ and let $E=\pi^{-1}(p)$ be its exceptional curve. Then $S'$ is an integral regular finite-type $k$-scheme of pure dimension two, $E$ is an exceptional curve of the first kind on $S'$ ([[def-exceptional-curve-and-contraction]]), and $\pi$ is a contraction of $E$. Moreover $\pi$ restricts to an isomorphism $S'\setminus E\to S\setminus\{p\}$.

Conversely, if $b\colon X\to X'$ is a contraction of an exceptional curve of the first kind, then $b$ is, up to unique isomorphism over $X$, the blowing up of a closed point of $X'$ with regular two-dimensional local ring.
items.strategy: Regularity, purity of dimension two and integrality of $S'$ are [[thm-blowup-regular-surface-closed-point-regular]] and [[cor-blowup-birational-integral-scheme]]; the exceptional curve is an effective Cartier divisor isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1_{\kappa(p)}$ with normal bundle $\mathcal O(-1)$ by [[lem-exceptional-curve-normal-bundle-minus-one]] and [[thm-pullback-center-ideal-invertible]]; the blowup is an isomorphism off the center by [[lem-blowup-isomorphism-off-center]]. So $\pi$ satisfies the definition of a contraction, and the converse half is the definition (b) of a contraction read backwards, with uniqueness from [[lem-universal-property-of-a-contraction]].

items.title: A function cutting the components of a special fibre
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$, $X$, $Y$, $f\colon X\to Y$ and $y\in Y$ be as in
[[lem-fibre-components-of-a-proper-birational-morphism-of-regular-surfaces]], and assume $\dim f^{-1}(y)=1$
with components $C_1,\dots,C_r$. Then there exists a nonzero element $u\in\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ such that for every
$i$ there is a closed point $x_i\in C_i$ with $x_i\notin C_j$ for $j\neq i$ and a factorization
$u=g_ih_i$ in $\mathcal O_{X,x_i}$ under the local homomorphism $f^\sharp\colon \mathcal O_{Y,y}\to\mathcal O_{X,x_i}$
in which $g_i\in\mathfrak m_{X,x_i}$ maps to a nonzero element of $\mathcal O_{C_i,x_i}$ and $h_i\in\mathcal O_{X,x_i}$.
items.strategy: Choose $x_i$ as in part (2) of the fibre-components lemma and choose any $g_i\in\mathfrak m_{X,x_i}$ whose image in $\mathcal O_{C_i,x_i}$ is nonzero. Since $f$ is birational, the fraction field of $X$ is the fraction field of $Y$ (part (3) of the same lemma), so $g_i=a_i/b_i$ with $a_i,b_i\in\mathcal O_{Y,y}$; set $u=\prod_j a_j$. In $\mathcal O_{X,x_i}$ this gives $u=g_i\cdot h_i$ with $h_i=b_i\prod_{j\neq i}a_j$, and $g_i$ still maps to a nonzero element of $\mathcal O_{C_i,x_i}$.

items.title: A proper birational map to a normal target is an isomorphism near a quasi-finite point
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $f:X\to S$ be a proper birational morphism of integral Noetherian schemes with normal $S$. If $f$ is quasi-finite at $x\in X$, then $f$ is an isomorphism over an open neighbourhood of $f(x)$; in particular that fibre consists of $x$.
items.strategy: Choose affine neighbourhoods of x and f(x), and shrink the source into its open quasi-finite locus. The coordinate algebra C is a domain inside the common function field K of the normal target algebra A. The relative integral closure of A in C is exactly A: every such element is integral over A and lies in K. The published source-local finite-algebra localization theorem therefore gives a principal neighbourhood of x with algebra A_g, since its finite intermediate algebra T contains A and lies in that integral closure. This is an open immersion into Spec(A); its inverse gives a section of f over D(g). A section of a separated morphism is a closed immersion, by base changing the closed diagonal. Its image contains the generic point of the integral scheme f^(-1)(D(g)); being closed, it is the whole underlying space. The defining ideal has radical zero and vanishes since the source is reduced. Thus the section is an isomorphism onto the entire inverse image, proving the result. No connected-fibre theorem or field-specific finite-birational statement is imported.

items.title: Regularity of a proper scheme transfers to and from local-base completion
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring and $X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ locally of finite type. Set $Y=X\times_A\widehat A$. For $y\in Y$ with image $x\in X$, regularity of $\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ implies regularity of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. If $y$ lies on the closed fibre, the two local rings are regular simultaneously. If $X$ is proper over $A$, then $X$ is regular if and only if $Y$ is regular. Here regular means that every local ring is regular; no smoothness over a field is asserted.
items.strategy: The map $A\to\widehat A$ is faithfully flat by thm-completion-of-a-noetherian-local-ring. Flatness survives base change and localization (tensoring and localizing are exact), so $\mathcal O_{X,x}\to\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ is a flat local map between Noetherian local rings. Descent in lem-ag-flat-local-regularity-ascent-descent gives the first assertion. On the closed fibre the preceding local-completion lemma identifies their completions; thm-completion-preserves-regular-local-rings gives the equivalence. If $X$ is proper, so is $Y$ by lem-proper-stable-base-change, and both are Noetherian. A closed point of either scheme maps to the closed point of its local base because a proper morphism is closed. Every point of a Noetherian scheme has a closed specialization: its closure is Noetherian and has a minimal nonempty closed subset, a closed point since scheme spaces are sober and T0. A local ring at the original point is a localization of the local ring at such a specialization, so cor-localisations-of-regular-local-rings-are-regular shows regularity can be checked at closed points. All these points are on the closed fibres, where the established equivalence applies. AC is inherited from the named suppliers.

items.title: Finite-length duality over a regular local base
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be regular Noetherian local of dimension $d$ and let $(B,\mathfrak n)$ be a module-finite local $R$-algebra with the map local. For finite-length $B$-modules put $T(M)=\operatorname{Ext}_R^d(M,R)$ with its natural $B$-action. Then $\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(M,R)=0$ for $i\ne d$, $T$ is exact contravariantly, $M\cong T(T(M))$ by canonical bidual evaluation, and $\operatorname{Ann}_B T(M)=\operatorname{Ann}_B M$.
items.strategy: A finite-length $B$-module has finite length over $R$: the residue extension is finite, and a $B$-composition series has factors finite-dimensional over $R/\mathfrak m$. A regular system of parameters of $R$ is a regular sequence generating $\mathfrak m$. Its Koszul resolution and its signed self-duality show $\operatorname{Ext}_R^i(R/\mathfrak m,R)=0$ except $i=d$, where it is $R/\mathfrak m$. Induct on an $R$-composition series of $M$, using the long exact Ext sequence, to get concentration in degree $d$ and exactness of $T$. Apply the preceding finite-base bidual lemma with $B$ and shift $s=d$: finite-ring adjunction identifies $R\operatorname{Hom}_B(M,D_B)$ with $R\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,R[d])$, which is precisely $T(M)$ in degree zero. Applying the adjunction a second time gives $M\cong T(T(M))$, as a $B$-module via the same evaluation. Multiplication by $b\in B$ on $T(M)$ is obtained contravariantly from multiplication on $M$; thus if it vanishes on $M$ it vanishes on $T(M)$, and conversely apply $T$ again and use bidual evaluation. Hence the annihilators agree. This supplies the exact finite-length duality and annihilator detection used in Stacks 54.8.8, without asserting general Matlis duality. DC is inherited from the long exact Ext sequence supplier. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: Relative derived duality on projective space over a regular local ring
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $R$ be regular Noetherian local of finite dimension and $P=\mathbb P^N_R$. Write $W=\mathcal O_P(-N-1)$. Laurent residue gives $t:R\Gamma(P,W[N])\to R$. For every $K\in D^b_{\mathrm{Coh}}(P)$, evaluation followed by $t$ gives a natural quasi-isomorphism $R\Gamma(P,\mathcal R\!Hom_P(K,W[N]))\cong R\operatorname{Hom}_R(R\Gamma(P,K),R)$. It respects shifts, triangles and multiplication by homogeneous sections.
items.strategy: Relative twisting-sheaf cohomology over the arbitrary ring $R$ is the actual published theorem: its standard-cover Laurent monomial complex decomposes as a direct sum over exponent vectors. A vector with some, but not all, negative entries has a contractible simplex complex; all-nonnegative vectors contribute degree zero and all-negative vectors contribute degree $N$. The residue on the unique all-minus-one vector defines $t$. For any twist $K=\mathcal O(m)$, the monomial pairing $x^a\cdot x^{-a-1}\mapsto1$ identifies the finite free degree-zero cohomology with the dual of the corresponding top cohomology, and all other groups vanish; it is compatible with polynomial multiplication by direct multiplication of Laurent monomials. The monomial complexes have the described contractible summands, so their derived global sections are their finite-free cohomology shifted appropriately; no exact duality over a field is assumed. Derived cup/evaluation and ordinary tensor-Hom adjunction on bounded finite-projective representatives produce the natural map in the statement. It is a quasi-isomorphism for twists, finite sums and shifts by the preceding calculation. Both sides are contravariant triangulated functors (the right side is **derived** Hom, not ordinary dual of arbitrary cohomology), so cones and the five lemma propagate this to finite twist resolutions and finite truncation triangles supplied by the preceding helper. For $N=0$ it is ordinary perfect-complex biduality over $R$. Chain evaluation and the signed total differential give shift/triangle compatibility, and the monomial calculation gives the required trace normalization. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: A normal-surface modification is an isomorphism in codimension one
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $f:X\to S$ be a modification of integral Noetherian schemes and let $S$ be normal of dimension two. Then $f$ is an isomorphism over an open subset containing every point of codimension at most one in $S$. The complement is a finite set of closed points. If every fibre is zero-dimensional, $f$ is an isomorphism. The union of curves contracted by $f$ is contained in the fibres over that finite set and is finite when $\dim X=2$.
items.strategy: At a codimension-one point $s$ the normal Noetherian local ring is a DVR by normality's R1 implication and the DVR supplier. Base-changing to its spectrum preserves properness and integrality (on affine charts this is localization); the generic inverse extends by the valuative criterion to a section of the proper morphism. A section of a separated morphism is a closed immersion: it is a base change of the closed diagonal. Its image contains the generic point and hence, being closed, all of the integral source; its defining ideal has radical zero and is zero because the source is reduced. Thus this base change is an isomorphism. The generic-point case is immediate. Around the fibre over $s$, the quasi-finite locus is open by its actual affine finite-type algebra supplier. The proper image of its closed complement is closed and misses $s$, so restrict the base away from that image. There the map is proper quasi-finite, hence finite. On an affine normal target its finite domain algebra lies integrally in the same fraction field, so equals the target algebra by integral closedness. This proves an isomorphism on a neighbourhood of $s$. The same construction gives the open union containing codimensions zero and one. Its closed complement is zero-dimensional in the Noetherian two-dimensional integral space, hence consists of finitely many closed points. If all fibres are zero-dimensional the whole morphism is proper quasi-finite and the same affine argument gives an isomorphism. If $\dim X=2$, each exceptional fibre is a proper closed subset of the integral two-dimensional space and has dimension at most one; it has finitely many irreducible components, and each contracted integral curve is a one-dimensional component of one of these finitely many fibres. No classical-variety finite-birational supplier is used outside its scope.

items.title: Surface non pth power detected by derivation
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $B$ be a domain of characteristic $p>0$ finite type over a complete equicharacteristic Noetherian local ring, and let $f\in B$ not be a $p$th power in $\operatorname{Frac}B$. There is a derivation $D:B\to B$ with $D(f)\ne0$.
items.strategy: Replace the base by its image, a complete local domain, and use its published finite power-series subring R. Generic Noether normalization gives R[Y]⊂B′⊂B with B′ finite over R[Y] and B′_g=B_g, g∈R nonzero: normalize over Frac(R), then replace each algebra generator x by g x to clear its monic equation. Replace f by g^(pN)f in B′. In L=Frac(B′), df is nonzero because the kernel of the universal absolute derivation is L^p (expand on a p-basis). The preceding separation lemma chooses J so df remains nonzero over K_J. A linear functional on the finite-dimensional differential space gives a K_J-derivation of L detecting f. Clear its values on finitely many A_J-module generators of B′ to obtain D′:B′→B′. Derivations extend to localization by D(a/s)=D(a)/s-aD(s)/s². If B′_g=B_g, multiply D′ by g^(N+1), where g^N times each B′-algebra generator of B lies in B′; the quotient formula proves that this derivation preserves B. Because the initial multiplier g^(pN) has derivative zero, the resulting derivation detects the original f. items.title: Positive canonical twists on projective Cohen–Macaulay curves
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $E$ be a projective pure CM curve over a field $\kappa$, with $H^0(E,O_E)=\kappa$ and canonical module $\omega_E$. If $L$ is globally generated and nontrivial, $H^1(E,\omega_E\otimes L)=0$. If $L$ is very ample with $\deg_\kappa L\ge2$, then $\omega_E\otimes L$ is globally generated. These statements allow nonreduced $E$.
items.strategy: Duality identifies H1(ω_E⊗L)∨ with Hom(ω_E⊗L,ω_E)=H0(L^-1), using canonical-module homothety. A nonzero section t of L^-1 and finitely many generators of L have some product st nonzero: otherwise the generators force t=0 locally. Since H0(O)=κ, that product is a nonzero scalar and trivializes L, contradiction. This proves vanishing. For generation, first pass to an algebraic closure. Field base change preserves H0(O)=κ, degree and generation by flat Čech cohomology; the ambient finite free polynomial resolutions identify the base change of ω_E with the canonical module. Pure CM survives field extension: at local rings flat-local depth additivity gives CM, since the zero-dimensional algebraic-extension fibres are CM and dimension is unchanged. Fix a closed geometric point e. Very ampleness gives a hyperplane section s vanishing at e and nonzero at every generic point of E: over the infinite algebraically closed field the hyperplanes through e that contain a given positive-dimensional component form a proper linear subspace; finitely many such subspaces cannot cover the parameter space. CM excludes embedded associated points, so s is regular. Let D=Z(s). Cartier coinduction from its two-term line-bundle resolution gives ω_D=(ω_E⊗L)|D, with finite-module duality at each Artinian stalk. The length of H0(ω_D) equals length of H0(O_D), which is deg L≥2 by the multiplication-by-s sequence and Euler-characteristic degree. Put F=ω_E⊗L. Its sequence 0→ω_E→F→ω_D→0 has quotient of dimension at least two and H1(ω_E) of dimension one. Let F′ be the subsheaf generated by global sections of F and the image of ω_E. Some global section has nonzero image in ω_D since the boundary has target dimension one. If H1(F′)≠0, the map H1(ω_E)→H1(F′) is an isomorphism. Serre duality representing H1(-)∨ supplies F′→ω_E whose composite with ω_E→F′ is the identity (homothety plus its nonzero action on H1). Thus F′ splits as ω_E plus a nonzero finite-support quotient, giving a nonzero finite-support subsheaf of the CM sheaf F, impossible. Therefore H1(F′)=0. If F/F′ were nonzero, the long exact sequence would surject H0(F) onto its nonzero finite-support global sections; this map is zero because every global section belongs to F′. Hence F′=F. The image of ω_E is sF, so at e the quotient by globally generated sections equals s times itself with s in the maximal ideal. Nakayama makes that quotient zero. Every closed point was arbitrary, proving generation, and faithful field base change descends it. The proof supplies the omitted finite-support and adjunction details in the source and does not assume E reduced or geometrically integral.

items.title: Quadratics in square ideals of colength greater than one
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. If $I\subset\kappa[x,y]$ has colength greater than one and contains a nonzero polynomial $q$ of total degree at most two in $I^2$, then $q$ is a scalar times the square of an affine linear polynomial. Infinite colength is allowed.
items.strategy: The two partial derivatives of q belong to I by Leibniz. A nonzero constant derivative would force I to be the unit ideal. If a nonconstant linear derivative is nonzero, make an affine coordinate change to put x∈I. Then I=(x) or (x,F(y)) with F monic of degree at least two. Modulo x², the x-coefficient of an element of I² is divisible by F and its constant-in-x part divisible by F². The degree bounds force both parts of q to vanish, leaving q=constant·x². If both derivatives vanish, characteristic is two and q=a+dx²+fy². A nonzero constant polynomial cannot lie in a proper I²; if only one variable occurs, differentiating its nonsquare scalar coefficient yields a unit in I unless the scalar ratio is a square, after which the result holds. Otherwise normalize f=1. If a and d are both squares, q is already a square. If d=s² and a is nonsquare, the change z=y+sx gives q=a+z², reducing to the one-variable case and contradiction. Thus the remaining two-variable nonsquare case has d nonsquare; choose a p-basis derivation θ with θ(d)≠0 before setting α=θ(a)/θ(d). Applying θ to q gives θ(a)+θ(d)x²∈I, hence x²+α∈I and y²+a+dα∈I. Then J=(x²+α,y²+a+dα)⊂I, and κ[x,y]/J has basis 1,x,y,xy. Since q is a nonzero linear combination of the two regular-sequence generators of J, it is not in J² (their conormal classes are a free basis, directly by division by their monic separate-variable polynomials). Thus I/J≠0. If it contains any nonzero vector with zero xy coefficient, I contains a nonzero affine linear polynomial and the earlier case applies. Otherwise I/J is one-dimensional and I has colength three. Extend scalars to an algebraic closure and translate x,y to make J=(x²,y²). Its one-dimensional added ideal is spanned by g+hx+iy+jxy with j≠0. If g≠0 it is a unit in that local four-dimensional algebra; if h or i is nonzero its ideal contains two independent vectors, so the quotient has length at most two. Both contradict length three. Thus Ibar=(x²,xy,y²). Its square has no nonzero polynomial of degree at most two, contradicting q∈Ibar². This excludes the remaining nonsquare case and proves the claim over the original field.

items.title: A divisor supported in a special fibre has positive conormal degree on some component
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$, $X$, $Y$, $f\colon X\to Y$ and $y\in Y$ be as in
[[lem-fibre-components-of-a-proper-birational-morphism-of-regular-surfaces]], and let $Z\subseteq X$ be a
nonzero effective Cartier divisor with $Z\subseteq f^{-1}(y)$ set-theoretically. Then there exists an
irreducible component $C$ of $Z$ with $\deg_C\bigl(\mathcal O_X(-Z)|_C\bigr)>0$; that is, the conormal sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(-Z)|_Z$ has a component of positive degree.
items.strategy: Write the one-dimensional fibre components as $C_j$. A cutter $u=g_jh_j$ has positive orders $e_j=v_{C_j}(u)$ and $g_j$ is nonzero on $C_j$ but vanishes at a chosen closed $x_j$ off all other components. Write $d_j=v_{C_j}(Z)$. Choose $i$ with $d_i/e_i$ maximal and replace $u$ by $u^{d_i}$ and $Z$ by $e_iZ$. The new orders satisfy $v_{C_j}(u)\ge v_{C_j}(Z)$ for every $j$, with equality at $i$; they are not asserted equal at all components. On the Cartier divisor $Z$, the section $u$ vanishes at each generic associated point, so it is zero by the no-embedded-points helper and belongs to its ideal $I$. It thus defines a section of $I|_{C_i}$ nonzero at the generic point. Near $x_i$ choose a local generator $t$ of $I$. The divisor has only the component $C_i$ there. Since $g_i$ is nonzero on that component and $Z$ has no embedded associated points, multiplication by $g_i$ on $\mathcal O_Z$ is injective. From $u=g_ih_i\in(t)$ it follows that $h_i\in(t)$; hence the section coefficient $u/t=g_i(h_i/t)$ vanishes at $x_i$. The proper integral-curve degree helper now gives positive degree for the rescaled conormal bundle. Additivity of degree on tensor powers divides out the positive scaling factor to give the original claim.

items.title: Projective coherent duality over a regular local base
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $R$ be regular Noetherian local of dimension $d$, let $X$ be projective over $R$, and fix $i:X\hookrightarrow P=\mathbb P^N_R$. Put $D_X=i^!(\mathcal O_P(-N-1)[N+d])$. Then $D_X$ is a dualizing complex on $X$, with coherent biduality. For every bounded coherent complex $K$ on $X$, trace/evaluation gives $R\Gamma(X,\mathcal R\!Hom_X(K,D_X))\cong R\operatorname{Hom}_R(R\Gamma(X,K),R[d])$. The pairing, not just its vector-space shadow, is canonical for the supplied embedding.
items.strategy: The affine charts of $P$ are regular finite-dimensional polynomial rings over $R$. On a chart with ring $A$, $X$ has ring $A/I$ and the ambient twist is invertible. The actual regular-quotient biduality supplier applies over this regular ring, hence $i^!$ produces a local dualizing complex with coherent biduality. Coinduction uses the natural quotient action and evaluation at one, so the chart complexes glue. Uniform finite twist resolutions over $P$ bound coherence degrees, giving a bounded coherent global complex. Closed-immersion internal Hom adjunction identifies $i_*\mathcal R\!Hom_X(K,D_X)$ with $\mathcal R\!Hom_P(i_*K,\mathcal O_P(-N-1)[N+d])$, and closed-immersion cohomology comparison identifies global sections with those on $X$. Apply the preceding relative projective-space duality, shifted by $d$, to obtain the displayed quasi-isomorphism. Its evaluation trace is obtained by the coinduction counit followed by Laurent residue, so it is the actual compatible composition pairing. Coherent biduality holds locally by the regular-quotient supplier, hence globally. This proves the required projective regular-base complex duality; concentration into a single dualizing **module** on a normal two-dimensional modification is a separate remaining helper, not asserted from this formula alone. DC is retained from the used resolution and Ext suppliers; AC implies DC.

items.title: Surface generic power series formal fibres
items.statement: Assume AC. For $A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]][Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]$ and $K=\operatorname{Frac}A$, every completed local generic fibre $\widehat{A_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_AK$ is geometrically regular over $K$.
items.strategy: It is regular before purely inseparable base change because A is regular and regularity survives completion and localization. In characteristic zero finite extensions are separable and preserve regularity. In characteristic p test finite purely inseparable extensions by degree-p towers M⊂M[z]/(z^p-f). Choose a finite A-subalgebra B⊂M with fraction field M and f∈B by clearing denominators with pth powers. B and B[z]/(z^p-f) have unique primes over p since their fraction-field extensions are purely inseparable. The finite-completion-factor lemma identifies A_p^hat⊗M with B_r^hat⊗_B M. Inductively it is regular. The detecting-derivation lemma gives D:B→B with D(f) nonzero; extend through localization, completion, and localization. Its value on f is a unit because it lies in M×. The hypersurface lemma proves regularity after the next degree-p step. This proves geometric regularity by the finite purely inseparable test. items.title: Surface open regular locus
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Every finite-type algebra over a field or a complete equicharacteristic Noetherian local ring has open regular locus. Thus the regular locus of any scheme locally of finite type over one of these bases is open.
items.strategy: First every complete local domain has a nonempty regular open. It is finite over a regular power-series subring; induct on fraction-field degree. Separable steps become standard étale after choosing a separating primitive element and clearing its equation/discriminant denominators. Degree-p steps are B[z]/(z^p-b) on a nonempty open: a detecting derivation of B has nonzero D(b), and invert D(b) and the denominator identifying the actual finite algebra with this hypersurface. The hypersurface lemma gives regularity. For any finite purely inseparable extension of a residue fraction field of the complete base, choose a finite subalgebra in that field; it is a complete local domain and has a regular open. For a finitely generated field extension K/k, enlarge k and K by finite purely inseparable extensions until K/k is separably generated: choose a transcendence basis; adjoin pth roots of finitely many coefficients in the minimal polynomial of a degree-p inseparable generator, and pth roots of the basis variables; the inseparable degree strictly decreases, giving a finite induction. Therefore every finite-type domain S over the complete base has a regular open: choose a finite base subalgebra in k′ and a finite S-subalgebra of K′ with fraction field K′ (multiply its finitely many algebraic field generators by denominators to make them integral). Work on this finite domain extension, spread a separating transcendence basis plus primitive separable generator to a standard smooth open, and descend regularity by generic flatness (restrict the base also so the open map is faithfully flat). Finally for any prime P at which T_P is regular, choose generators f_i of P_P forming a regular sequence; their generation and regularity spread to an open. On V(P), a nonempty regular open of T/P lifts to a regular open of T by the regular-sequence quotient criterion. The regular locus is stable under generalization, and this condition on every irreducible closed subset implies openness by Noetherian induction. Spreading a regular sequence is justified by its successive multiplication kernels: they are finite modules and vanish at the chosen prime, so one denominator kills each kernel; generation of P is spread by the same finite-module argument on P/(f_i). Regularity lifts from the quotient successively by the published regular-element lifting theorem. For generic-flat descent of a regular source open, apply generic freeness to that localized algebra over the domain base; it becomes a nonzero free module, hence faithfully flat (the algebra is nonzero and injection at the generic point guarantees at least one basis element). Published flat-local regular descent then applies. The topological criterion follows by Noetherian induction: on every irreducible closed set the regular locus is empty if its generic point is absent (generalization stability), and otherwise contains a nonempty relative open; induction on the remaining proper closed subset proves constructibility. A constructible generalization-stable subset of a Noetherian space is open, as its specialization-stable constructible complement is closed. items.title: Surface complete equicharacteristic finite integral closure
items.statement: Assume AC. The integral closure of a complete equicharacteristic Noetherian local domain in every finite extension of its fraction field is a finite module.
items.strategy: Use the finite regular power-series subring R. For a finite separable extension of Frac(R), choose an integral power basis and use the nondegenerate trace pairing: traces of products of integral elements are integral and belong to R because R is normal; invert one discriminant to place every integral element in one finite R-module. In characteristic p first pass to a finite normal envelope and its maximal purely inseparable subextension. Handle that subextension by degree-p induction. At a step, the preceding normalization B is finite over R, normal and Noetherian. For L=Frac(B)[z]/(z^p-b), b∈B not a pth power, choose D:B→B with D(b)≠0. If u=sum_(j≤i) a_j z^j is integral, differentiate u^p∈B. Its derivative is the pth power of sum_(j≥1) j D(b) a_j z^(j-1), up to the harmless factor D(b)^(p-1), so that sum is integral. Inducting on i gives D(b)^i a_j∈B; the constant coefficient follows by subtraction and normality. All integral elements lie in sum_(j<p) B D(b)^(-(p-1))z^j, hence form a finite B-module. Separable trace finiteness then applies to the normal envelope. Integral closure in the desired intermediate field is a submodule of its finite closure; transitivity of integrality identifies closure of the original domain with closure of R. No Tate or mixed characteristic input is needed. Regular power-series rings are normal: they and all prime localizations are regular and Cohen–Macaulay, hence R1/S2; apply the published domain Serre criterion. The trace of an integral element is integral since it is the sum of its conjugates in a finite normal envelope (with the usual multiplicity); its trace lies in the base fraction field and hence in the normal base. The inseparable induction uses v=sum_(j≥1)j D(b)a_j z^(j-1) with v^p=D(b)^(p-1)D(u^p)∈B, so v is integral; the displayed bound follows exactly without assuming D preserves arbitrary integral closures. items.title: Dimension and cohomology of local normal surface modifications
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a normal Noetherian local domain of dimension two and $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ an integral modification. Then $X$ has dimension two, all closed points have local dimension two, $f$ is an isomorphism off the closed point, $f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A}$, and its special fibre has dimension at most one. If $X$ is projective over $A$, it has a cover by two affine opens, hence $H^q(X,F)=0$ for $q>1$ for every quasi-coherent $F$. In particular $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$ has finite length over $A$.
items.strategy: Normality and dimension two make $A$ CM. At a closed point $x$ of $X$, properness puts it on the closed fibre with finite residue extension. On an affine chart write its domain algebra $C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_N]/I$. The polynomial local ring at $x$ is CM of dimension $N+2$: flat-local depth additivity gives depth $2+N$, and lifting parameters from $A$ and the polynomial closed fibre gives dimension at most $2+N$, while depth is at most dimension. The prime $I$ avoids nonzero $A$-elements; localizing at those elements identifies chains below it with those below a maximal prime of $\operatorname{Frac}(A)[t]$ whose residue field is the common function field. Thus its height is $N$. The CM local codimension formula makes $\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}=2$. All points specialize to closed points, so all local dimensions are at most two; the scheme dimension is two. The codimension-one modification helper gives the isomorphism off $\mathfrak m$. Every affine target open has finite structure-sheaf pushforward by proper coherent finiteness. Its algebra embeds into the common function field and is integral over the normal target ring, hence equals that ring. A component of the special fibre of dimension two would be the whole integral surface, contradicting the generic isomorphism, so its dimension is at most one. For projective $X$, choose an ample embedding bundle $L$. Pick one closed point on each one-dimensional component of the fibre and a sufficiently high twist section nonzero at each: restriction to these finitely many points is onto by Serre vanishing for their ideal. Its zero set on the fibre is finite. Raise this section to a high power and choose a second section of the same twist nonzero at every point of that finite zero set, again by the finite restriction sequence and Serre vanishing. Their common-zero locus is proper over the local base and misses the closed fibre, hence is empty. Include these sections in a finite generating system of that very ample twist (the original embedding sections and its Veronese powers suffice); their nonvanishing opens are closed in affine charts of projective space, so affine. They cover $X$; their intersection is affine by separatedness, so the Čech complex has length one. Proper coherent finiteness and the isomorphism off $\mathfrak m$ make $H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)$ finite supported at the maximal ideal, hence finite length. If the fibre is zero-dimensional the same argument uses any first section nonzero on its finite set; no positive-dimensional component is assumed.

items.title: Degree-p differential trace extends across normal surface valuations
items.statement: Assume AC and DC. Let $Y\xrightarrow\pi X$ be a finite dominant morphism of normal integral Noetherian schemes of characteristic $p$ whose function fields have purely inseparable degree $p$. If $\Omega_{X/S}$ is coherent, then for $q\ge1$ the generic differential trace extends canonically to $\pi_*\wedge^q\Omega_{Y/S}\to(\wedge^q\Omega_{X/S})^{**}$. For a monogenic algebra $B=A[z]/(z^p-f)$ it kills forms pulled back from $A$ and sends $\eta\wedge z^i dz$ to zero for $i<p-1$ and to $\eta\wedge df$ for $i=p-1$.
items.strategy: Define the monogenic differential trace by the coefficient of z^(p−1)dz. Prove generator independence using a universal polynomial identity: the low powers give zero coefficient by ordinary differentiation; the top coefficient is computed by lifting universal coefficients to Z, dividing the formal derivative by p there, then reducing mod p—never using p⁻¹ in characteristic p. At each height-one DVR the degree-p extension is monogenic by the ramification/residue-degree cases and Nakayama, so the trace is integral on regular forms. The double-dual codimension-one criterion extends the generic map canonically.
